title: Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters
intro: This guide sets out who may represent a party in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice and family court, where the sources on this site say legal help and information can be found, and what they say about language rights and interpreters.

sections.heading: Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court
paragraphs: The Courts of Justice Act says “A party may be represented in a proceeding in the Small Claims Court by a person authorized under the Law Society Act to represent the party”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 26)

The same section lets the court exclude a representative from a hearing. The court may exclude “anyone, other than a person licensed under the Law Society Act, appearing on behalf of the party if it finds that such person is not competent properly to represent the party, or does not understand and comply at the hearing with the duties and responsibilities of an advocate.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 26)

Steps to Justice says “You do not have to hire a lawyer or paralegal when you go to Small Claims Court.” It also says “both lawyers and paralegals can represent you in Small Claims Court. However, only a lawyer can represent you in Superior Court, or the Court of Appeal.” (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)

That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017; the family court section below sets out what the Family Law Rules now say about family legal services providers. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)

sections.heading: Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice
paragraphs: Under the Rules of Civil Procedure, “A party to a proceeding who is under disability or acts in a representative capacity shall be represented by a lawyer.” A party that is a corporation “shall be represented by a lawyer, except with leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (1), (2))

Every other party has a choice: “Any other party to a proceeding may act in person or be represented by a lawyer.” This includes a lawyer “acting under a limited scope retainer”, but such a retainer “does not, in itself, make a lawyer the lawyer of record for the party.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (3), (4))

When a party acts in person, “anything these rules require or permit a lawyer to do shall be done by the party.” A party acting in person may appoint a lawyer of record by serving and filing a notice of appointment of lawyer (Form 15B) (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01.1 (1), 15.03 (2), (3))

Subject to the rules that require some parties to have a lawyer, a party with a lawyer of record may elect to act in person by serving and filing a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01.1 (1), 15.03 (2), (3))

sections.heading: Who can represent a party in family court
paragraphs: Under the Family Law Rules, a party may “act in person”, “be represented by a lawyer”, or, “if the court gives permission in advance, be represented by any other person, on terms set out by the court.” (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1))

A party may also be represented by a “family legal services provider” in a limited list of cases and matters “as authorized under the Law Society Act”. The list includes an uncontested divorce or one started by a joint application where the only claim is for divorce, filing a domestic contract, a change of name application, some child support motions, and some enforcement of support. Each item has its own conditions, set out in the rule. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1) (c))
This does not apply “if the court determines that representation by a family legal services provider is inappropriate in the circumstances” (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (0.1), (1.2), (1.4), (1.5))

A lawyer or family legal services provider may act under a limited scope retainer, which the rules define, for a lawyer, as legal services for “part, but not all, of a party’s case, by agreement” and, for a family legal services provider, as “some, but not all, of the services that a family legal services provider is authorized to provide in a party’s case or matter”. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (0.1), (1.2), (1.4), (1.5))

A party acting in person may choose a licensed representative “by serving on every other party and filing a notice of change in representation (Form 4) containing the consent of the licensed representative to act.” This is not needed for a limited scope representative who is not the representative of record (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (9), (9.1), (10), (10.1))

A represented party may use Form 4 to change representatives or act in person, but in a child protection case scheduled for trial or on a trial list, acting in person needs the court’s permission in advance. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (9), (9.1), (10), (10.1))

sections.heading: Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario
paragraphs: Steps to Justice explains that “Lawyers can give legal advice. This means they can explain what the law says and how it applies to your situation.” A paralegal “is another kind of legal professional that can give legal advice about Small Claims Court.” It says “a paralegal is not allowed to work in all the legal areas that a lawyer can.” That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)

“The Law Society of Ontario regulates lawyers and paralegals in Ontario.” It has rules about who can become a lawyer or paralegal and how they must behave, and it deals with complaints. That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)

The Law Society Referral Service “can provide you with the name of a lawyer or paralegal in your area, who will provide a free initial consultation of up to 30 minutes to help determine your rights and options.” A request can be made through the online form at www.lawsocietyreferralservice.ca. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

For people unable to use the online service, “A crisis line is available Monday to Friday, 9:00 am to 5:00 pm.” The number given is 416-947-5255 (toll free 1-855-947-5255). The Law Society also has a Lawyer and Paralegal Directory at www.lawyerandparalegal.directory. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)

Some lawyers offer “unbundled services” or “limited scope retainer” services: “This means you pay them to help you with part of your case.” Examples given are summary advice, preparing documents, appearances, and coaching on the court process. Steps to Justice says “Some lawyers and paralegals do not charge for the first meeting.” (Steps to Justice, How do I prepare for my meeting with a lawyer or paralegal?)

A complaint can be made to the Law Society only if a lawyer or paralegal “did not do their job properly, or behaved unprofessionally.” The Law Society does not deal with legal fees. A complaint must be made “within 3 years of when the problem happened or when you became aware of it.” The page adds that there is no time limit for a complaint about sexual abuse. (Steps to Justice, How do I complain to the Law Society of Ontario about a lawyer or paralegal?)

sections.heading: Free and low-cost help for Small Claims matters
paragraphs: Steps to Justice lists these next steps for legal help with a Small Claims issue: “Find a lawyer or paralegal”, “Get help from Pro Bono Ontario”, “Contact JusticeNet” and “Call a community legal clinic”. That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)

“If you earn a low income, you might be able to get legal help from Pro Bono Ontario . Pro Bono Ontario helps with cases in Small Claims Court and Superior Court.” (Steps to Justice, How can I sue in Small Claims Court?)

“PBO has a hotline where you can get up to 30 minutes of free legal advice.” Steps to Justice also says “PBO offer services in some court locations in Toronto and Ottawa”; that page was last reviewed on July 14, 2022. (Steps to Justice, What happens at my Small Claims Court trial?; Steps to Justice, I filed a claim with the Small Claims online service. What happens next?)
“If you earn a low income, a community legal clinic might be able to help you with your case.” (Steps to Justice, I filed a claim with the Small Claims online service. What happens next?)

“The Small Claims Court Guided Pathways is a free online tool that asks you questions and puts your answers into the required court forms.” The page also points to Community Legal Education Ontario (CLEO) and Steps to Justice for more information about Small Claims Court. (ontario.ca, File Small Claims Court documents online)

sections.heading: Finding help for a Superior Court civil matter
paragraphs: The Ontario government page on filing civil claims says a person without a lawyer can find one through the “Law Society of Ontario's referral service or directory of lawyers” or through “Pro Bono Ontario , if you can't afford a lawyer and need help with a civil matter”. (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)

Steps to Justice says that suing for more than $50,000 must be done in Superior Court, and that a person owed more than $50,000 who is “willing to waive the amount over $50,000” can still file in Small Claims Court. (Steps to Justice, How can I sue in Small Claims Court?)

sections.heading: English, French and interpreters
paragraphs: “The official languages of the courts of Ontario are English and French.” Unless French-language rules apply, hearings are in English and “evidence adduced in a language other than English shall be interpreted into the English language”. Documents filed must be in English or come with a translation “certified by affidavit of the translator.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 125)

Pleadings and other documents filed by a party may be written in French. “A party to a proceeding who speaks French has the right to require that it be conducted as a bilingual proceeding”. The hearings the party specifies are then “presided over by a judge or officer who speaks English and French.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 126 (1), (4))

The Ontario government says “You have the right to use a court interpreter if you or a witness are deaf or do not understand the language of the proceeding.” A person with a fee waiver “can request the help of a court interpreter for free for any language other than English or French”, using form FW-A 5. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

Without a fee waiver, “you are responsible for booking and paying for interpreter services for yourself or for your witness.” A fee waiver is not needed for an English-French or French-English interpreter in a civil, family or small claims court matter. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

sections.heading: Interpreters for witnesses, by court
paragraphs: Small Claims Court: “If a party serves a summons on a witness who requires an interpreter, the party shall arrange for a qualified interpreter to attend at the trial unless the interpretation is from English to French or French to English and an interpreter is provided by the Ministry of the Attorney General.” If not, every other party may request an adjournment of the trial, with costs. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.03 (5.1), (5.2))

The Ministry’s guide adds that for a summonsed witness “the court will provide an interpreter from English to French or French to English or visual language interpretation.” It also says “The court will provide an interpreter for other languages to parties who have qualified for a fee waiver.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)

Superior Court: where a witness does not understand the language of the examination or is deaf or mute, “the party calling the witness shall provide the interpreter, unless the interpretation is to be from English to French or from French to English and an interpreter is provided by the Ministry of the Attorney General.” A similar rule applies at oral examinations. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.01 (5), (6), 34.09)

Family court, divorce proceedings: under the Divorce Act, a proceeding “may be conducted in English or French, or in both official languages of Canada.” The court “shall, at the request of any person, provide simultaneous interpretation from one official language into the other”. The site does not yet have a source on the Family Law Rules for interpreters in other languages. (Divorce Act, s. 23.2)

sections.heading: What the site does not have a source for yet
paragraphs: The sources on this site do not yet cover duty counsel, the services of Legal Aid Ontario, Family Law Information Centres, or how to ask a courthouse for a disability-related accommodation. The only related item found is a note that court forms in alternative formats can be requested by email at attorneygeneral@ontario.ca. (Ontario Court Forms, Rules of the Small Claims Court Forms)
